beats.role_note: why care — stated before the CLI loop begins; SHOW-DON'T-TELL LAW: Manim, not a static card
beats.narration_text: A general analytics interview tests joins, cohorts, dashboards — skills you already have. A banking one adds a second language on top: regulators like the OCC and the CFPB, ratios like CET1 and LCR, and an instinct for the question every bank case eventually asks — is this number regulatory-reportable, and could it be fraud. Miss that layer, and a technically perfect answer still reads as "never worked in banking."
beats.visual_intent: SQL and Python tiles slide in and lock together (a skillset already solid); a second, translucent layer of terms — CET1 · LCR · OCC · CFPB · charge-off — slides in on top and snaps opaque, labeled 'the layer banking adds'

beats.role_note: the book's own map — six parts
beats.narration_text: This book maps that layer in six parts: the regulatory landscape, the risk and governance rules that generate it, the modern data stack it lives in, forty-plus worked SQL and Python problems on real banking patterns, the behavioral and case rounds that test judgment, and a one-page day-of cheat sheet.
beats.visual_intent: six labeled blocks build left-to-right into a single pipeline (Landscape → Regulation/Risk → Data Stack → Technical Prep → Behavioral/Case/Systems → Day-Of), each locking in with a soft snap as its name is spoken

beats.narration_text: Take one worked problem from the book: chapter eight's running balance — six months of end-of-month balances, built one CTE at a time.

props.command: claude "review this running-balance query — six months of end-of-month balances, one CTE at a time"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 1, the correct query (Ch.8, no bug reconstruction)
beats.narration_text: Here's the shape. A running CTE computes the cumulative balance over the whole ledger — no WHERE clause at all. One CTE later, last posting per month narrows down to the reporting window and picks each month's last posting. Sum first. Filter after. Get that order backwards, and the balance comes out silently wrong.

props.title: running_balance.sql
props.code:
WITH running AS (
    SELECT account_id, transaction_id, posted_at,
        SUM(amount) OVER (
            PARTITION BY account_id
            ORDER BY posted_at, transaction_id
            ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
        ) AS running_balance
    FROM transactions
    -- no WHERE here — the sum must see the whole ledger
),
last_posting_per_month AS (
    SELECT account_id,
        DATE_FORMAT(posted_at, '%Y-%m-01') AS month_start,
        running_balance,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY account_id, DATE_FORMAT(posted_at, '%Y-%m')
            ORDER BY posted_at DESC, transaction_id DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM running
    WHERE posted_at >= '2026-01-01'
      AND posted_at <  '2026-07-01'
)
SELECT account_id, month_start, running_balance
FROM last_posting_per_month
WHERE rn = 1;

beats.narration_text: Run it: this account carried twelve thousand four hundred dollars into January, from a deposit made the year before. End-of-month balances land at twelve-one, twelve-two-fifty, twelve-one-seventy-five — the true balance, because the running total saw the whole ledger first.
beats.visual_intent: 3-row EOM table builds top-to-bottom (Jan/Feb/Mar), each value landing in teal: 12,100.00 / 12,250.00 / 12,175.00; small annotation ties Jan's value back to the Nov 2025 deposit crossing the year boundary

beats.narration_text: Two moves, same discipline: get the SQL evaluation order right, and never lose the cohort. That's chapters eight and nine. The rest of the book applies the same discipline to regulatory metrics, the modern data stack, and the behavioral and case rounds banks actually run.
